summary.name: Continuous integration
summary.one_liner: Wikipedia article describing continuous integration (CI), the practice of frequently merging code changes into a shared branch and automatically building and testing the result.
use_cases: understanding CI practices for a development team
setting up automated builds and tests on each commit
reducing merge conflicts from long-lived branches
learning the history of continuous integration
summary.what_it_does: The page explains continuous integration as a development practice: developers merge changes to a shared integration branch frequently, and an automated system builds and tests the codebase, often on every commit or once a day. It covers core practices such as single-command builds, atomic commits, committing at least daily, fixing bugs with accompanying test cases, keeping builds fast, and testing in a production-like staging environment. It also outlines the relationship between CI, continuous delivery and continuous deployment, plus benefits and risks. A history section traces the term to Grady Booch in 1991 and to Extreme Programming, CruiseControl (2001) and IMVU's continuous deployment work.
notable: Covers CI history from Grady Booch (1991) and Extreme Programming through CruiseControl (2001)
Lists practical guidelines such as daily integration, every-commit builds and test-with-bug-fix rules
Links to a comparison of continuous integration software and related articles
caveats: Describes a practice rather than a single tool; it is a general encyclopedia article
Some sections are flagged as needing expansion or more citations
Lists risks such as setup effort, test quality dependence and high build latency
